summary: Hostnames, URIs, IP addresses, and email addresses are often compared when making security decisions. If different parties use different comparison algorithms, the result can be a security hole. This informational document discusses these identifier comparison issues.

plainLanguage.summary: If two people check names differently, a trick can fool one and not the other. This warns about those mix-ups.

questions: why comparing hostnames and uris is risky
why is identifier comparison a security risk
what is a false positive in identifier comparison
what are absolute definite and indefinite identifiers
subtitle: When systems compare names in different ways, attackers can slip through the gap.

tldr.problem: Hostnames, URIs, email addresses and other identifiers are compared when making security decisions, and different parties often use different comparison rules.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC classifies identifiers as Absolute, Definite or Indefinite, explains how false positives and false negatives become privilege escalation or denial of service, and walks through trouble spots in hostnames, ports, URIs and email addresses.
tldr.outcome: New identifiers should specify an Absolute or Definite comparison algorithm, and designers combining several protocols should check that their comparison rules agree.

today: RFC 6943 is an Informational document from the IAB and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Identifiers and How They Are Matched
sections.content:
Identifiers name humans, devices, content and more. Three processes matter: the identifier is generated, distributed and used. Each step can use a different form of the identifier (printed, spoken, electronic), and each use involves matching a user-supplied identifier against a repository, so matching can be complicated. The document compares two identifiers to see whether they are the same identifier, not whether they refer to the same entity.

Identifiers fall into three classes. Absolute identifiers are compared byte by byte, such as binary IP addresses. Definite identifiers have a single well-defined comparison algorithm, such as URI scheme names, which are case-insensitive US-ASCII. Indefinite identifiers have no single algorithm, such as human names.

The most common method is canonicalization: convert each identifier to a canonical form and compare bitwise. All parties must agree on the same algorithm.
sections.plainLanguage: Names can be written, said or typed in different ways. To check whether two names are the same, everyone has to agree on one way to tidy them up first.

sections.title: How Mismatches Become Attacks
sections.content:
Identifiers drive authentication, authorization and accounting. If the parties use different matching algorithms for the same identifiers, results range from denial of service to elevation of privilege.

A false positive is when two different things compare as equal. A false negative is when the same thing compares as different. Their worst effects depend on the policy: with grant on match, a false positive elevates privilege and a false negative denies service; with deny on match, it is reversed. Elevation of privilege is almost always seen as far worse, so URI comparison in RFC 3986 is designed to minimize false negatives while strictly avoiding false positives. URIs therefore fit grant-on-match systems, not deny-on-match ones.

The RFC gives a hypothetical case. Foo Corp's canonicalizer counts the URI fragment and example.com's ignores it. A malicious employee registers the account alice#stuff, obtains a token for it, and presents that token for alice, which example.com treats as a match.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a guard who checks names with a loose rule and a clerk who checks with a strict rule. A trickster can pick a name that the clerk thinks is new but the guard thinks is someone else's.

sections.title: Trouble Spots in Common Identifiers
sections.content:
Hostnames are ambiguous: the word can mean a fully qualified domain name, the leftmost label, and so on, so whether "example" equals "example.com" depends on the definition. IPv4 literals have a loose form (octal, hexadecimal, fewer than four parts, as accepted by inet_addr()) and a strict form (inet_pton()). So "10.11.12" may be an address or a hostname. URIs resolve this by allowing only the strict form. IPv6 literals have many equivalent string forms, which is why comparing binary addresses is safer. Internationalized names add encodings such as Punycode A-labels and percent-encoding, and a hostname starting with xn-- can be ambiguous.

Comparing names by resolving them to IP addresses is unreliable because of dynamic and private addresses and location-dependent DNS answers, and it leaks information about security decisions.

URIs have component-specific issues: unrecognized schemes cannot be safely compared, userinfo may or may not count, paths are case sensitive unless a scheme says otherwise, query order and empty queries are unspecified, and fragments are typically ignored for security comparison. Email address-like identifiers have a local part left for each domain to define, so they are typically Indefinite.
sections.plainLanguage: The same house can be written in many ways: with or without a number, in capital letters or small ones, in another alphabet. A careful guard has to know which ways count as the same.

sections.title: General Issues
sections.content:
Conflation means one string could be one of several identifier types, such as an IP literal or a hostname, or a port number or a service name. Such strings are Definite only if the syntaxes are disjoint or a precedence rule decides. Reserving the otherwise inaccessible space can keep things unambiguous.

Internationalization raises further problems. The DNS cannot tell whether two strings look equivalent to a human, and visually confusable strings make visual inspection unreliable for security. A string should be validated after, or as part of, canonicalization, or an attacker could inject delimiters such as @ or . through percent encoding, NFKC or non-shortest-form UTF-8.

Scope matters when an identifier such as localhost is not globally unique. Temporality matters when identifiers are reassigned, so stale entries in access control lists or caches can cause problems.
sections.plainLanguage: A name like "Mum" only works inside one family, and a phone number can later belong to someone new. Both can fool a guard who forgets the context.

sections.title: Recommendations
sections.content:
Systems that need both allow and deny operations within the same identifier space should avoid Indefinite identifiers in security comparisons. New identifiers should specify an Absolute or Definite comparison algorithm, resolving ambiguities such as "standard dotted decimal". If extensibility is allowed, as with new URI schemes, the comparison algorithm should stay the same so unrecognized extensions can still be compared. Some issues can be mitigated by treating unrecognized identifiers as invalid.

The hardest case is several protocols with different comparison algorithms working together. Designers should study those differences to understand the risks; dealing with them in current systems is left as future work.
sections.plainLanguage: When you invent a new kind of name, write down exactly how to compare two of them, so nobody can play tricks with the gaps.
